planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines or rooted cuttings in early spring on a trellis or trained support.

directions: Brought to Uruguay from southwest France in the 1870s by Basque settler Pascual Harriague, this thick-skinned, deeply tannic red variety found conditions in Uruguay's clay-limestone soils even more hospitable than its homeland and has since become the country's signature grape, far outproducing its original Madiran region. Train vines on a trellis with good air circulation, since the tight, productive clusters and dense foliage are prone to fungal pressure in Uruguay's humid summers. Prune hard each winter to limit yields and concentrate the variety's naturally high tannin and color; thinning leaves around the fruit zone in midsummer improves ripening in cooler vintages. Harvest when seeds turn brown and skins darken fully, as underripe Tannat is notoriously astringent, while fully ripe fruit produces the dense, dark, age-worthy reds Uruguay is now known for.
sources: Estudio comparativo de clones comerciales de Tannat (Vitis vinifera L.) en el sur del Uruguay

planting.note: Transplant container-grown seedlings in spring once frost risk has passed; the spiny trunk makes later relocation difficult, so site it thoughtfully from the start.

directions: Mbocayá is a tough, spine-covered palm of the open savannas and grasslands of eastern Paraguay, northern Argentina, and the Mato Grosso do Sul region of Brazil, where it has been harvested from wild and semi-wild stands commercially since the mid-20th century. The hard-shelled, golf-ball-sized fruit yields an oily, fibrous orange pulp and a rich kernel, both pressed for cooking and cosmetic oil in Paraguayan household and small-industry use, while the sweetish pulp itself can be eaten fresh or fermented into chicha. Grow in full sun on lean, well-drained savanna-type soils; established palms tolerate drought, poor fertility, and occasional light frost far better than most oil-bearing palms, but young plants need protection from hard freezes. Because the trunk is armed with dense black spines and fruiting does not begin for many years, plant it well away from walkways and give it room to mature undisturbed.
sources: Facultad de Ciencias Agrarias, Universidad Nacional de Asunción — Acrocomia totai research
Gesellschaft für Erhaltung alter und gefährdeter Haustierrassen / Hohenheim Acrocomia brief

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Guabiroba grows wild across the gallery forests and grassland edges of Paraguay, Uruguay, northern Argentina, and southern Brazil, where its small, round, yellow-green to orange fruit is gathered for fresh eating and widely used to flavor juice, ice cream, and liqueurs. The tree tolerates cooler nights and brief light frost better than most tropical myrtle-family fruits, making it workable at the warm edge of temperate gardens as well as in true subtropical climates. Plant in deep, moisture-retentive soil and water regularly through establishment, since the species naturally grows along stream edges and forest margins rather than dry open ground. Harvest fruit as it softens and turns from green to yellow-orange, picking promptly since ripe fruit drops quickly and bruises easily; the thin skin and aromatic, slightly tart pulp are both edible.
sources: Instituto Misionero de Biodiversidad — Guabiroba (Campomanesia xanthocarpa)
